Think Fast, Plan Selectively: Adaptive Deliberation for Efficient Data-Driven MPC

Yi Xian Goh Affiliation: Independent Researcher Email: gohyixian456@gmail.com    Sze Jue Yang Affiliation: Faculty of Computer Science and Information Technology, Universiti Malaya Email: jasonyang429@um.edu.my    Hao Luan Affiliation: School of Computing, National University of Singapore Email: haoluan@comp.nus.edu.sg
Abstract

Data-driven model predictive control (MPC) combines learned world models with online trajectory optimization, achieving strong performance in continuous control. However, the per-step cost of sampling and evaluating hundreds of candidate trajectories restricts deployment to control frequencies well below what real-time robotics demands. Motivated by the dual-process theory of human cognition, which distinguishes between fast, intuitive processing (System 1) and slower, deliberative reasoning (System 2), we ask whether every decision requires the same degree of computational deliberation. We propose Fast-TD-MPC, a lightweight framework that adaptively routes between fast policy execution and test-time planning, reserving costly deliberation for states where it is most needed. Fast-TD-MPC delivers competitive task performance across 103 continuous control tasks while achieving up to ∼4×{\sim}4\times faster inference. Under external disturbances, Fast-TD-MPC selectively falls back to planning, maintaining robustness comparable to the original planner.

   

1 Introduction

Data-driven Model Predictive Control (MPC) combines learned world models with online trajectory optimization, achieving state-of-the-art performance across diverse domains (Hansen et al., 2024; Hafner et al., 2025; Schrittwieser et al., 2020). By learning to predict environment dynamics, world models (Ha and Schmidhuber, 2018) unlock test-time planning: the ability to propose, evaluate, and optimize candidate action sequences before execution, rather than reactively mapping states to actions (Hansen et al., 2022; Schrittwieser et al., 2020; Wang et al., 2025). This planning capability consistently outperforms purely reactive policies and enhances robustness in dynamic environments, driving progress in robotic manipulation and locomotion (Hansen et al., 2024; Hafner et al., 2025; Hafner et al., 2020; Nagabandi et al., 2018; Hafner et al., 2019), autonomous driving (Guan et al., 2024; Liu et al., 2026b), and game-playing (Schrittwieser et al., 2020).

Planning brings robustness, but at the cost of substantial per-step computation. At each decision step, a planner samples and evaluates hundreds of candidate trajectories, resulting in per-step latencies that exceed the control frequencies required for real-time robotic deployment and latency-sensitive tasks (Dong et al., 2025; Gangapurwala et al., 2023). When planning is slow relative to changes in the environment, the state for which an action was planned may have already changed by the time it is executed, resulting in stale-action errors (Cheng et al., 2026; Lin et al., 2025b).

This raises a natural question: does every decision require the same amount of deliberation?

In most control problems, the answer is unlikely to be yes (Kahneman, 2011; Fridovich-Keil et al., 2018; Graves, 2016). Large portions of observations are familiar, and the action trajectories given such observations are predictable. Under such circumstances, a learned, reactive policy with low latency can already provide reliable actions; repeatedly invoking a full planner for these routine observations offers little benefit relative to its cost. Planning becomes more valuable when the agent encounters unfamiliar observations, disturbances, or situations where its learned behavior is less reliable. However, many test-time planners that utilize a learned world model devote the same computational budget to every timestep, ignoring the fact that not all decisions require planning.

A similar distinction arises in human decision-making. Dual-process theory (Kahneman, 2011; Daw et al., 2005; Botvinick et al., 2009) describes two complementary modes of thought: (i) a fast, intuitive System 1 that handles familiar situations through learned experience, and (ii) a slower, deliberative System 2 that reasons through complex or novel situations. Humans naturally alternate between both systems for effective decision-making.

Motivated by this view, we propose Fast-TD-MPC, a framework that dynamically switches between fast reactive execution and test-time planning. Applied to TD-MPC2 (Hansen et al., 2024), Fast-TD-MPC uses the original Model Predictive Path Integral (MPPI) planner as System 2 (the slow but robust fallback), a compact amortized neural network trained via planner imitation as System 1 (the fast, reflexive policy), and a lightweight out-of-distribution (OOD) detector as the gating mechanism (Figure 1). When the current observation is familiar, System 1 provides a reliable action at low latency; when the observation is OOD, System 2 is triggered to deliberate and plan. Since the detector itself costs negligible computation, the effective per-step latency scales linearly with the fraction of timesteps that require planning.

Our contributions are threefold:

  • •

    We introduce Fast-TD-MPC, a framework for adaptive test-time planning in data-driven MPC. Applied to TD-MPC2 (Hansen et al., 2024), it combines the original MPPI planner as a robust System 2 with a compact policy trained through planner imitation as a fast System 1, gated by a lightweight OOD detector, without modifying the underlying world model or planner.

  • •

    We conduct extensive evaluations across 103 continuous-control tasks spanning four domains: DMControl (Tassa et al., 2018) (physics simulated locomotion and manipulation), Meta-World (Yu et al., 2019) (multi-object manipulation), ManiSkill2 (Gu et al., 2023) (robotic manipulation), and MyoSuite (Caggiano et al., 2022) (physiologically realistic musculoskeletal motor control). Fast-TD-MPC achieves up to ∼4×{\sim}4\times inference speedup (∼2.7×{\sim}2.7\times on average) with <10%{<}10\% performance drop on 3 of 4 domains, using a single set of hyperparameters across all tasks (Figure 2).

  • •

    We show that faster decision-making does not come at the expense of robustness. Under five disturbance types spanning three categories, Fast-TD-MPC selectively falls back to planning when the agent encounters out-of-distribution states, retaining 95% of TD-MPC2’s perturbed return on DMControl at half its latency.

2 Preliminaries

Problem formulation.

We consider the standard infinite-horizon Markov Decision Process (MDP) (Puterman, 1990) setting, characterized by a tuple (𝒮,𝒜,T,R,γ,p0)(\mathcal{S},\mathcal{A},T,R,\gamma,p_{0}), where s∈𝒮s\in\mathcal{S} and a∈𝒜a\in\mathcal{A} are continuous states and actions, T:𝒮×𝒜→𝒮T:\mathcal{S}\times\mathcal{A}\to\mathcal{S} is the transition (dynamics) function, R:𝒮×𝒜→ℝR:\mathcal{S}\times\mathcal{A}\to\mathbb{R} is a reward function associated with a particular task, γ∈[0,1)\gamma\in[0,1) is a discount factor, and p0p_{0} is the initial state distribution. The goal is to derive a control policy π:𝒮→𝒜\pi:\mathcal{S}\to\mathcal{A} such that the expected discounted sum of rewards (return) 𝔼π[∑t=0∞γt​rt],rt=ℛ⁡(st,π⁡(st))\mathop{\mathbb{E}}_{\pi}\left[\sum_{t=0}^{\infty}\gamma^{t}r_{t}\right],\quad r_{t}=\mathcal{R}(s_{t},\pi(s_{t})) is maximized. In practice, each step must complete within the environment’s control cycle; slow per-step computation incurs stale-action errors and degraded return.

TD-MPC2.

Our work builds on TD-MPC2 (Hansen et al., 2024), an algorithm that combines test-time planning in a latent space using MPC (Negenborn et al., 2005) with actor-critic Temporal Difference (TD) learning. TD-MPC2 consists of five components as follows (θ\theta denotes all learnable parameters, dzd_{z} the latent state dimensionality, dad_{a} the action dimensionality):

  • •

    An encoder ℰθ:𝒮→ℝdz\mathcal{E}_{\theta}:\mathcal{S}\to\mathbb{R}^{d_{z}} mapping a state ss to its latent representation z=ℰθ​(s)z=\mathcal{E}_{\theta}(s).

  • •

    A latent dynamics model 𝒟θ:ℝdz×𝒜→ℝdz\mathcal{D}_{\theta}:\mathbb{R}^{d_{z}}\times\mathcal{A}\to\mathbb{R}^{d_{z}}, predicting the next latent z^′=𝒟θ​(z,a)\hat{z}^{\prime}=\mathcal{D}_{\theta}(z,a).

  • •

    A reward predictor ℛθ:ℝdz×𝒜→ℝ\mathcal{R}_{\theta}:\mathbb{R}^{d_{z}}\times\mathcal{A}\to\mathbb{R}, computing expected rewards r^=ℛθ​(z,a)\hat{r}=\mathcal{R}_{\theta}(z,a).

  • •

    A policy prior πθ:ℝdz→𝒜\pi_{\theta}:\mathbb{R}^{d_{z}}\to\mathcal{A}, a stochastic maximum-entropy policy that guides planning, from which actions a∼πθ(⋅∣z)a\sim\pi_{\theta}(\cdot\mid z) are sampled.

  • •

    A critic Qθ:ℝdz×𝒜→ℝQ_{\theta}:\mathbb{R}^{d_{z}}\times\mathcal{A}\to\mathbb{R}, estimating state-action values Qθ​(z,a)≈Qπθ​(s,a)Q_{\theta}(z,a)\approx Q^{\pi_{\theta}}(s,a). TD-MPC2 trains an ensemble of NQ=5N_{Q}=5 critics and computes TD-targets as the minimum of two randomly subsampled target critics to mitigate value overestimation.

The world model components ℰθ\mathcal{E}_{\theta}, 𝒟θ\mathcal{D}_{\theta}, ℛθ\mathcal{R}_{\theta}, and QθQ_{\theta} are jointly optimized by minimizing a combined objective over sub-trajectories of horizon HH sampled from a replay buffer ℬ\mathcal{B}:

ℒ(θ)≐𝔼(s,a,r,s′)0:H∼ℬ[∑t=0Hλt(‖z^t′−sg⁡(ℰθ−​(st′))‖2⏟joint-embedding prediction+CE⁡(r^t,rt)⏟reward prediction+CE⁡(q^t,qt)⏟value prediction)],\mathcal{L}(\theta)\doteq\mathop{\mathbb{E}}_{(s,a,r,s^{\prime})_{0:H}\sim\mathcal{B}}\left[\sum_{t=0}^{H}\lambda^{t}\left(\underbrace{\|\hat{z}^{\prime}_{t}-\mathrm{sg}(\mathcal{E}_{\theta^{-}}(s^{\prime}_{t}))\|^{2}}_{\text{joint-embedding prediction}}+\underbrace{\mathrm{CE}(\hat{r}_{t},r_{t})}_{\text{reward prediction}}+\underbrace{\mathrm{CE}(\hat{q}_{t},q_{t})}_{\text{value prediction}}\right)\right], (1)

where z^t\hat{z}_{t} are recurrently predicted latents (z^0=ℰθ​(s0)\hat{z}_{0}=\mathcal{E}_{\theta}(s_{0}), z^t′=𝒟θ​(z^t,at)\hat{z}^{\prime}_{t}=\mathcal{D}_{\theta}(\hat{z}_{t},a_{t})), sg\mathrm{sg} is the stop-gradient operator, θ−\theta^{-} are target parameters updated as an exponential moving average (EMA) of θ\theta, λ∈(0,1]\lambda\in(0,1] is a temporal coefficient that down-weights distant predictions, qt≐rt+γ​Q¯​(zt′,πθ​(zt′))q_{t}\doteq r_{t}+\gamma\bar{Q}(z^{\prime}_{t},\pi_{\theta}(z^{\prime}_{t})) is the TD-target with Q¯\bar{Q} being an EMA of the critic ensemble, and CE\mathrm{CE} denotes cross-entropy with soft two-hot targets in a symlog-transformed discrete space.

The policy prior πθ\pi_{\theta} is trained independently by maximizing:

ℒπ(θ)≐𝔼(s,a)0:H∼ℬ[∑t=0Hλt[αQθ(zt,πθ(zt))+βℋ(πθ(⋅∣zt))]],\mathcal{L}_{\pi}(\theta)\doteq\mathop{\mathbb{E}}_{(s,a)_{0:H}\sim\mathcal{B}}\left[\sum_{t=0}^{H}\lambda^{t}\left[\alpha\,Q_{\theta}(z_{t},\pi_{\theta}(z_{t}))+\beta\,\mathcal{H}\!\left(\pi_{\theta}(\cdot\mid z_{t})\right)\right]\right], (2)

where ℋ\mathcal{H} is the policy entropy and α,β\alpha,\beta are coefficients balanced via moving statistics to prevent premature entropy collapse. Gradients of ℒπ\mathcal{L}_{\pi} are taken only with respect to the parameters of πθ\pi_{\theta}.

At inference time, TD-MPC2 plans in the latent space using MPPI (Williams et al., 2015). Let μ,σ∈ℝH×da\mu,\sigma\in\mathbb{R}^{H\times d_{a}} be the parameters of a time-dependent multivariate Gaussian with diagonal covariance. Given the current state sts_{t} of a decision step tt, the encoder produces zt=ℰθ​(st)z_{t}=\mathcal{E}_{\theta}(s_{t}), and MPPI iteratively refines the parameters (μ,σ)(\mu,\sigma) over action sequences of horizon HH by (i) sampling NN candidate trajectories, including a fraction from the policy prior πθ\pi_{\theta}; (ii) evaluating each via latent rollout and terminal value bootstrapping:

J^=γH​Qθ​(zH,πθ​(zH))+∑h=0H−1γh​ℛθ​(zh,ah);\hat{J}=\gamma^{H}Q_{\theta}(z_{H},\pi_{\theta}(z_{H}))+\sum_{h=0}^{H-1}\gamma^{h}\mathcal{R}_{\theta}(z_{h},a_{h}); (3)

and (iii) updating (μ,σ)(\mu,\sigma) via an importance weighted average over top-kk elite trajectories, yielding refined parameters (μt∗,σt∗)(\mu^{*}_{t},\sigma^{*}_{t}). Only the first action at∼𝒩⁡(μt∗,σt∗2)a_{t}\sim\mathcal{N}(\mu^{*}_{t},\sigma^{*2}_{t}) is executed, and the process repeats the next decision step, with μt∗\mu^{*}_{t} shifted by one position to warm-start the next iteration’s sampling. We refer readers to their paper for exact algorithmic details.

3 Fast-TD-MPC: A Framework for Adaptive Test-Time Planning

We study accelerating TD-MPC2 inference while preserving its robustness to states outside the expert distribution. Given a pre-trained TD-MPC2 world model (with frozen parameters θ\theta), our goal is to route each decision step to the fastest system capable of handling it, without significantly degrading return. Fast-TD-MPC consists of three components, all frozen prior to deployment (Figure 1): (i) an amortized policy (System 1), (ii) the MPPI planner (System 2), and (iii) an OOD gate.

System 1: Amortized Policy.

Planner amortization reduces the per-step cost of MPPI by training a lightweight feed-forward policy πS1\pi_{\text{S1}} to imitate the planner. Given expert demonstrations 𝒟exp={(zt,at∗)}\mathcal{D}_{\text{exp}}=\{(z_{t},a^{*}_{t})\} collected via planner rollouts, we minimize the imitation objective: min⁡𝔼(z,a∗)∼𝒟expϕ⁡[ℓ⁡(πS1​(z,ϕ),a∗)]\min_{\phi}\;\mathop{\mathbb{E}}_{(z,a^{*})\sim\mathcal{D}_{\text{exp}}}\left[\ell\!\left(\pi_{\text{S1}}(z;\phi),\,a^{*}\right)\right], where ϕ\phi are the parameters of πS1\pi_{\text{S1}} and ℓ\ell is an L1 loss, with |a^−a∗||\hat{a}-a^{*}| denoting the element-wise absolute difference summed over dad_{a}. See Appendix K for training and architectural details. While this reduces inference to a single forward pass, the amortized policy cannot recover from states outside the expert distribution. We address this via OOD detection.

System 2: MPPI Planner.

We use TD-MPC2’s world model and MPPI planning algorithm (Section 2) as-is. When the gate switches from System 1 to System 2 after KK timesteps, the warm-start buffer is KK-step stale. We explicitly zero the buffer on System 1 to System 2 transitions, forcing a cold start from the policy prior πθ\pi_{\theta}, which provides fresh forward-looking candidates via the world model. The planner resumes normal warm-starting on subsequent consecutive System 2 steps.

OOD Gating.

To address the failure mode of the amortized policy, we employ out-of-distribution (OOD) detection (Hendrycks and Gimpel, 2017; Lee et al., 2018) in the latent space. We employ Mahalanobis distance (Mahalanobis, 1936) as the scoring function: g⁡(zt)=(zt−z¯)⊤​Σreg−1​(zt−z¯)g(z_{t})=(z_{t}-\bar{z})^{\top}\Sigma_{\text{reg}}^{-1}(z_{t}-\bar{z}), where z¯\bar{z} and Σ\Sigma are the mean and full covariance of in-distribution (ID) latents, fitted offline with ℓ2\ell_{2} shrinkage (Σreg=Σ+λ​𝐈\Sigma_{\text{reg}}=\Sigma+\lambda\mathbf{I}, λ=0.01\lambda=0.01). To construct the ID set, we roll out πS1\pi_{\text{S1}} and collect all visited latents {zt}\{z_{t}\}. We consider two labeling modes: (i) theoretical, where all visited states are treated as ID, and (ii) reward-gated, where a state is labeled ID only if its per-step rewards meet or exceed the average per-step counterparts of TD-MPC2 expert rollouts at the same timestep. The gating is then:

at={πS1​(zt,ϕ)if ​g​(zt)≤τ,πS2​(st,θ)if ​g​(zt)>τ,a_{t}=\begin{cases}\pi_{\text{S1}}(z_{t};\phi)&\text{if }g(z_{t})\leq\tau,\\ \pi_{\text{S2}}(s_{t};\theta)&\text{if }g(z_{t})>\tau,\end{cases} (4)

where τ\tau controls the speed–robustness trade-off. For theoretical mode, τ\tau defaults to the median11 1 Under Gaussian assumptions, the squared Mahalanobis distance follows a χ2\chi^{2} distribution (Mahalanobis, 1936), which is right-skewed; the median is therefore more representative of the typical score than the mean. of all scores on a held-out validation set. For reward-gated mode, τ\tau defaults to the midpoint between the median scores of the ID and OOD partitions. We additionally sweep multiple percentile values and report the full Pareto frontier in Section 4.2.

Latency Profile.

Since g⁡(zt)g(z_{t}) is a single matrix-vector product, the overhead of OOD detection is negligible. The effective per-step latency is: ttotal≈ℰθ+g+ρ⋅πS2+(1−ρ)⋅πS1+tenvt_{\text{total}}\approx\mathcal{E}_{\theta}+g+\rho\cdot\pi_{\text{S2}}+(1{-}\rho)\cdot\pi_{\text{S1}}+t_{\text{env}}, where ρ\rho is the S2 invocation rate, πS2≫πS1\pi_{\text{S2}}\gg\pi_{\text{S1}}, and ℰθ\mathcal{E}_{\theta}, gg, and tenvt_{\text{env}} are incurred at every step. As ρ→0\rho\to 0, the system approaches the speed of a purely amortized policy; as ρ→1\rho\to 1, it approaches the robustness of full planning. The threshold τ\tau directly controls this trade-off.

Algorithm.

Algorithm 1 summarizes the full inference procedure. All components are computed offline and frozen at deployment.

4 Experiments

We seek to address the following research questions:

  • •

    RQ1: Can Fast-TD-MPC achieve substantial inference speedup over TD-MPC2 without significant degradation in return or success rate across diverse continuous control tasks?

  • •

    RQ2: Can Fast-TD-MPC preserve the robustness of the original TD-MPC2 system under various disturbances?

We additionally analyze the speed-robustness trade-off via τ\tau and ablate the MPPI planner warm-start strategy and OOD distance metric.

4.1 Experimental Setup

We evaluate Fast-TD-MPC across 103 continuous control tasks spanning 4 domains: DMControl (Tassa et al., 2018), Meta-World (Yu et al., 2019), ManiSkill2 (Gu et al., 2023), and MyoSuite (Caggiano et al., 2022), with action spaces up to 𝒜∈ℝ39\mathcal{A}\in\mathbb{R}^{39} and diverse tasks from manipulation to complex locomotion. We consider the single-task setting with 3 seeds per task. All Fast-TD-MPC components are fitted independently for each task-seed pair using a single set of hyperparameters across all tasks; no per-task tuning done. See Appendix C and K for task and hyperparameter details.

Baselines.

We compare against 5 TD-MPC2-derived baselines: (i) S2-alone (full TD-MPC2, N=512N{=}512), (ii) S2-reduced (N=64N{=}64), (iii) S2 policy-only (no MPPI), (iv) S1 alone (amortized MLP), (v) Round-robin (S2 invoked at a fixed rate of 50%, 33%, 20%, or 10%). We evaluate 2 OOD modes (theoretical and reward-gated) across multiple τ\tau percentiles, and reference DreamerV3 (Hafner et al., 2025) and SAC (Haarnoja et al., 2018) numbers from Hansen et al. (2024). We follow Hansen et al. (2024)’s evaluation setup, and report return/success rate, per-step latency (ms), S2 invocation rate (ρ\rho), as well as peak GPU memory. Refer Appendix H for hardware and evaluation details.

4.2 Speedup vs. Performance (RQ1)

We present aggregate results in Tab. 1 and Fig. 2, with per-component latency breakdowns in Tab. 2.

Pareto-optimal speed–performance trade-off.

At τp​50\tau_{p50}, Fast-TD-MPC (all) matches TD-MPC2 within the 95% CI across all domains (829 vs. 820 on DMControl, 85% vs. 84% on Meta-World) while reducing latency by ∼1.3{\sim}1.3–1.4×1.4\times (27.3 ms →\to 19.4 ms on DMControl, 45.9 ms →\to 33.9 ms on ManiSkill2). Varying τ\tau traces a Pareto frontier: at τp​75\tau_{p75}, speedup reaches ∼2×{\sim}2\times (27.3 ms →\to 12.2 ms on DMControl, and 45.9 ms →\to 23.3 ms on ManiSkill2); at τp​90\tau_{p90}, Fast-TD-MPC achieves ∼2.7×{\sim}2.7\times average speedup (up to 4.2×4.2\times on DMControl) with <10%{<}10\% performance drop on 3 of 4 domains, retaining 96% of TD-MPC2’s return on DMControl, matching its success rate on Meta-World, and retaining 93% on MyoSuite. Beyond p90p_{90}, performance degrades sharply: at τp​99\tau_{p99}, DMControl return drops to 650 (∼20%{\sim}20\% loss) and ManiSkill2 success to 20%, as the gate routes nearly all steps to System 1, reducing to the S1-alone regime.

State-aware gating vs. fixed scheduling.

Round-robin (RR) invokes System 2 at a fixed rate regardless of state. On DMControl, gating dominates every RR operating point at matched latency, e.g., 785 return at 6.5 ms (τp​90\tau_{p90}) vs. 743 at 6.6 ms (RR 20%), and 745 at 3.8 ms (τp​95\tau_{p95}) vs. 699 at 4.0 ms (RR 10%). On ManiSkill2, the two are comparable: gating is ahead at intermediate latency, with 47% at 23.3 ms (τp​75\tau_{p75}) vs. 42% at 22.3 ms (RR 33%), while RR 50% is stronger at the high-latency end (60% at 28.4 ms vs. 54% at 33.9 ms for τp​50\tau_{p50}). On Meta-World, all scheduling variants lie within 2 points (84–86%), indicating saturation. On MyoSuite, RR (S2 10%) recovers TD-MPC2’s success (40%) at 6.6 ms, whereas the gate still invokes S2 on 60% of steps at τp​90\tau_{p90}. Thus, which timesteps are planned matters most when only a small subset of states requires planning; otherwise, fixed scheduling is a simpler alternative.

OOD mode comparison.

The reward-gated mode matches the theoretical mode’s performance at lower latency across multiple domains. On Meta-World, RG τp​50\tau_{p50} achieves 85% at 10.0 ms vs. all τp​90\tau_{p90}’s 85% at 12.2 ms. On MyoSuite, RG τp​75\tau_{p75} achieves 39% at 15.7 ms, matching all τp​50\tau_{p50}’s 39% at 31.4 ms and exceeding all τp​90\tau_{p90}’s 37% at 22.6 ms. This suggests reward-gating’s tighter ID distribution produces a more precise threshold, reducing unnecessary S2 invocations on states System 1 can reliably handle.

Reference baselines.

Both DreamerV3 and SAC are faster than TD-MPC2 but achieve lower returns, particularly on DMControl (735 and 631 vs. 820) and MyoSuite (14% and 38% vs. 40%). Among TD-MPC2-derived baselines, reducing the planner’s sample budget (N=512N{=}512 →\to N=64N{=}64) degrades return on DMControl by 22% and MyoSuite by 40%, while providing little latency reduction, as latency is dominated by fixed GPU overhead rather than sample count. S1 alone achieves the lowest latency but degrades significantly, particularly on ManiSkill2 (19% vs. 65%) and DMControl (623 vs. 820), confirming that pure amortization without a fallback is insufficient. The policy-only variant (no MPPI) is similarly fast but performs worse than S1 on most domains, confirming that supervised distillation from MPPI yields a stronger reactive policy than the TD-MPC2 actor alone.

Runtime breakdown.

Table 2 details the per-component latency breakdown. The OOD gate adds negligible overhead (∼\sim0.2 ms), while System 1 is ∼\sim65×\times cheaper per invocation than System 2 (∼\sim0.4 ms vs. ∼\sim26 ms on H100). At τp​50\tau_{p50}, ρ\rho adapts to domain difficulty (81% on H100 vs. 66% on A100), and peak GPU memory remains bounded by S2-alone.

Latency scales linearly with planning frequency.

Figure 3 confirms that per-step latency scales linearly with ρ\rho across all domains (R2≥0.93R^{2}\geq 0.93), validating the runtime model: since the OOD detector costs negligible computation (∼0.2{\sim}0.2 ms), total latency is determined by the fraction of timesteps routed to System 2. Both all and RG modes fall on the same line, confirming that τ\tau controls only the operating point along this line, not the per-step cost structure.

4.3 Robustness Under Disturbances (RQ2)

We evaluate 102 of the 103 tasks under five types of externally applied disturbances, organized following the taxonomy of Gu et al. (2025) into three groups: (i) observation (observation noise: additive Gaussian on sts_{t}), (ii) action (action noise: additive Gaussian on ata_{t}), (iii) environment (velocity kick: instantaneous impulse on qvelq_{\text{vel}}; gravity shift: sustained rescaling of gravity; sustained force: continuous injection with probability p=0.15p{=}0.15). We report results for the combined setting, which applies all five disturbances simultaneously. All disturbances are applied post-training at evaluation time with per-episode stochasticity. See Appendix E for full details including the excluded task.

We compare against (i) S2-alone, (ii) S2 policy-only, (iii) S1 alone, and (iv) Round-robin (50%), measuring absolute performance and degradation relative to the undisturbed setting. We present aggregate results across all 4 domains in Table 3 and Figure 4.

Speed–performance trade-off holds under disturbances.

At τp​90\tau_{p90}, Fast-TD-MPC (all) retains 95% of TD-MPC2’s perturbed DMControl return (586 vs. 616) at 2×2\times speedup, while on ManiSkill2, τp​50\tau_{p50} achieves 66% success at 34.6 ms vs. TD-MPC2’s 66% at 43.1 ms. On Meta-World, all methods degrade to a similar level (47–51%), leaving little room to separate them.

OOD gating preserves robustness.

Perturbations degrade TD-MPC2 substantially (−25%-25\% return on DMControl, −39%-39\% success on Meta-World), and S1 alone even more (−35%-35\% and −46%-46\%), indicating that the amortized policy is more sensitive to distribution shift than the planner. At τp​50\tau_{p50}, where the gate routes most perturbed steps to the planner (88% on DMControl, 99% on Meta-World), Fast-TD-MPC (all) tracks TD-MPC2 closely: 617 vs. 616 on DMControl, 51% vs. 51% on Meta-World, 66% vs. 66% on ManiSkill2, and 36% vs. 40% on MyoSuite. This robustness stems from adaptive routing rather than a fixed planning budget: at τp​90\tau_{p90}, the S2 invocation rate rises from 18% to 45% on DMControl and from 39% to 82% on Meta-World under perturbation (Appendix G). Figure 5 illustrates this at the step level: a velocity kick at step 312 pushes g⁡(zt)g(z_{t}) above τ\tau, triggering S2 for several steps before the system resumes S1.

State-aware gating vs. fixed scheduling under disturbances.

Under perturbation, Fast-TD-MPC matches or slightly exceeds RR 50% at a lower latency on DMControl (586 at 13.6 ms vs. 577 at 14.5 ms, τp​90\tau_{p90}) and ManiSkill2 (62% at 25.9 ms vs. 58% at 27.1 ms, RG τp​25\tau_{p25}), although differences lie within the 95% CIs. The key difference is adaptivity: the same τp​90\tau_{p90} configuration runs at 6.5 ms per step on clean DMControl episodes and increases planning only when perturbed, whereas RR 50% spends 14.4 ms per step in both conditions and degrades more (813→577813\to 577, −29%-29\%, vs. 785→586785\to 586, −25%-25\%). On Meta-World and MyoSuite, RR is on par with or better than gating at matched latency.

Reward-gated mode under disturbance.

The reward-gated mode’s efficiency advantage on Meta-World and MyoSuite (Section 4.2) persists under perturbation. On Meta-World, RG τp​50\tau_{p50} and τp​75\tau_{p75} reach 49-50% at 17.4-18.9 ms, faster than any all configuration (the fastest, τp​99\tau_{p99}, reaches 50% at 20.2 ms). On MyoSuite, RG τp​75\tau_{p75} achieves 35% at 17.7 ms, comparable to all τp​50\tau_{p50} (36% at 32.2 ms) and above all τp​90\tau_{p90} (34% at 22.9 ms). In both cases, gains come from fewer S2 invocations (e.g., 44% vs. 60–89% on MyoSuite), suggesting that reward-gating’s tighter ID distribution produces a more precise threshold, reducing unnecessary S2 invocations on states System 1 can reliably handle.

4.4 Ablations

MPPI Planner Warm-Start Strategy.

We compare cold starting the MPPI planner against KK-shifted warm start, which salvages the first H−KH{-}K steps of the stale buffer when K<H−1K<H{-}1 and cold-starts otherwise. A paired t-test across all task-config comparisons on all 4 benchmark domains finds no significant difference (p>0.05p>0.05) in return (t=1.31t{=}1.31, p=0.19p{=}0.19) or S2 invocation rate (t=−0.28t{=}{-}0.28, p=0.78p{=}0.78). Under disturbance, return (t=−0.78t{=}{-}0.78, p=0.44p{=}0.44) and S2 rate (t=1.35t{=}1.35, p=0.18p{=}0.18) remain insignificant. We adopt cold start for its simplicity. See Appendix I for full results.

OOD distance metric.

We compare Mahalanobis and Tanimoto distance (Rogers and Tanimoto, 1960) for OOD gating. A paired t-test across all task-config comparisons finds no significant difference in nominal return (t=0.85t{=}0.85, p=0.40p{=}0.40). In the theoretical mode, Tanimoto yields equal or lower latency at every τ\tau percentile, but degrades robustness: under perturbation, Mahalanobis achieves significantly higher return (t=2.33t{=}2.33, p=0.02p{=}0.02) by routing more timesteps to the planner. We therefore adopt Mahalanobis distance as the OOD gating. See Appendix J for full results.

5 Limitations and Discussions

We identify three main limitations. First, the OOD gate is reactive. It detects atypical states only after they are visited, rather than anticipating them from the learned dynamics model. A predictive gate could pre-route to System 2 before state degradation occurs, further reducing wasted computation on unrecoverable trajectories. Second, while the default τ\tau is set by a fixed rule on held-out OOD scores, the optimal threshold varies across domains (e.g., locomotion vs. manipulation); real-world deployment may require tracing the Pareto frontier to identify a task-appropriate operating point. Finally, all experiments are conducted in simulation, while sim-to-real gaps exist for realistic robotic systems; we defer real-robot validation to future work.

6 Related Work

Data-Driven MPC and TD-MPC2.

TD-MPC2 (Hansen et al., 2024) combines latent dynamics modeling with MPPI planning and TD-learning, achieving state-of-the-art performance across 104 continuous control tasks, outperforming SAC (Haarnoja et al., 2018) and DreamerV3 (Hafner et al., 2025). Its ecosystem addresses training efficiency (Evers et al., 2026), humanoid locomotion (Nguyen et al., 2025; Nguyen et al., 2026b), and world model reliability (Hansen and Wang, 2026). Fast-TD-MPC builds on this framework but targets inference-time acceleration.

Accelerating Test-Time Planning.

Approaches to reducing the per-step cost of MPPI fall into four categories: (i) Model reduction distills the planner into a smaller or quantized model, but MPPI still runs at every step (Kuzmenko and Shvai, 2025; Wang et al., 2025); (ii) Planner acceleration speeds up the planning loop itself (e.g., parallelizing latent rollouts (Gao and Xu, 2026)) but does not eliminate it; (iii) Full amortization replaces the planner entirely with a feed-forward policy (Nguyen et al., 2026a), achieving large speedups but providing no fallback when the policy encounters out-of-distribution states; (iv) Conditional replanning skips planning on some timesteps: Cheng et al. (2026) adapt replanning tolerance based on model mismatch by reusing cached plans, while Lin et al. (2025b) generate action queues from the planner’s own latent rollouts with full replanning on mismatch. Fast-TD-MPC differs by combining separately amortized full policy replacement with OOD-gated fallback to the complete planner. The amortized policy is distilled from expert planner rollouts, so the planning expertise is retained in the fast path, and only the iterative optimization at inference time is eliminated. Classical event-triggered control (Tabuada, 2007; Heemels et al., 2012) and the dual-process framework (Kahneman, 2011; Daw et al., 2005; Botvinick et al., 2009) provide broader intellectual context. See Appendix L for a detailed comparison.

7 Conclusion

We presented Fast-TD-MPC, a framework that accelerates TD-MPC2 inference by routing in-distribution states to a compact amortized policy and falling back to the full MPPI planner only when the OOD detector flags atypical states. Across 103 continuous control tasks spanning four domains, Fast-TD-MPC achieves up to ∼4×{\sim}4\times inference speedup (∼2.7×{\sim}2.7\times on average) with <10%{<}10\% performance drop on 3 of 4 domains, using a single set of hyperparameters. Under five combined external disturbance types, the gate adaptively increases planning on perturbed states, retaining 95% of TD-MPC2’s perturbed return on DMControl at half its latency. The framework is conceptually general: any model-based planner can serve as System 2, any amortized policy as System 1, and the gating decision reduces to a single transparent scalar comparison, a desirable property for safety-critical applications where auditability matters.

Appendix A Method Details

Algorithm 1 summarizes the full Fast-TD-MPC inference procedure. At each decision step tt, the frozen encoder ℰθ\mathcal{E}_{\theta} maps the current state sts_{t} to latent ztz_{t}, and the OOD detector computes the Mahalanobis distance g⁡(zt)g(z_{t}). If g⁡(zt)≤τg(z_{t})\leq\tau, the state is deemed in-distribution and the amortized policy πS1\pi_{\text{S1}} produces the action in a single forward pass. Otherwise, the full MPPI planner πS2\pi_{\text{S2}} is invoked. All components are frozen at deployment; the only runtime computation is the encoding, OOD scoring, and the selected policy’s forward pass.

Appendix B Task Visualizations

Appendix C Task Domains

We consider a total of 103 continuous control tasks from 4 task domains: DMControl (Tassa et al., 2018), Meta-World (Yu et al., 2019), MyoSuite (Caggiano et al., 2022), and ManiSkill2 (Gu et al., 2023). We provide an exhaustive list of all tasks considered, along with their details in Table 4, 5, 6 and 7 below. Visualizations of each task are provided in Appendix B. Environment details are provided in Appendix D and Appendix E.

Appendix D Environment Details

For experiments on RQ1, we follow Hansen et al. (2024)’s setup and benchmark on DMControl, Meta-World, ManiSkill2, and MyoSuite without modification. All four domains are infinite-horizon continuous control environments with fixed episode lengths and no termination conditions. We list episode lengths, action repeats, and the performance metric used for each domain in Table 8. Following Hansen et al. (2024), we adopt a strict success criterion: an episode is successful only if its final step is successful. In object manipulation tasks, this ensures that an episode in which an object is picked up but subsequently dropped is not counted as a success.

Appendix E Environment with Externally Applied Disturbances

For experiments on RQ2, we introduce five types of disturbances to all four benchmark domains. Table 9 details the five disturbance types, organized following the taxonomy of Gu et al. (2025) into observation, action, and environment disruptors, along with their categories and activation probabilities. All disturbances are applied post-training at evaluation time with per-episode stochasticity (seed = 42); per-episode parameters are drawn from the specified ranges using an isolated RandomState.

Excluded Task.

The pick-ycb task (PickSingleYCB-v0) from ManiSkill2 is excluded from the perturbation evaluation due to a SAPIEN (Xiang et al., 2020) memory management bug that triggers a C-level segfault when physics-based disturbances are applied to articulated YCB mesh objects. This is a known SAPIEN limitation unrelated to our method. All other ManiSkill2 tasks are unaffected.

SAPIEN Backend Adaptation.

ManiSkill2 environments are built on SAPIEN (Xiang et al., 2020), which exposes a different physics API than MuJoCo (Todorov et al., 2012). While observation noise and action noise operate on the observation and action arrays respectively (backend-agnostic), three perturbation types require adaptation: (i) Gravity shift: SAPIEN’s SceneConfig.gravity is a direct 3D vector, equivalent to MuJoCo’s model.opt.gravity. (ii) Velocity kick: applied via set_qvel(get_qvel() + impulse). (iii) Sustained force: SAPIEN does not expose qfrc_applied; we implement this as per-step velocity injection, set_qvel(get_qvel() + 𝐟\mathbf{f}), producing equivalent trajectory disruption with the same magnitude and direction sampling.

Appendix F Full Results

Tables 10 – 13 present the full benchmark results for each domain, including per-step latency, S2 invocation rate (ρ\rho), and peak GPU memory, complementing Table 1. Tables 14 – 17 provide per-task breakdowns for four key methods.

Appendix G Full Results under Disturbances

Tables 18 – 21 present the full results under disturbances for each domain, including per-step latency, S2 invocation rate (ρ\rho), and peak GPU memory, complementing Table 3. Tables 22 – 25 provide corresponding per-task breakdowns.

Appendix H Evaluation Setup and Hardware Details

Evaluation Metrics.

We follow Hansen et al. (2024)’s setup of training on 3 seeds and evaluating on the same 3 seeds, with 1 warmup + 10 evaluation episodes per task per seed. We report return/success rate, per-step latency (ms), S2 invocation rate (ρ\rho), and peak GPU memory.

Hardware.

Per-step latency is measured with GPU synchronization at the start and end of each decision step (2 syncs), on a single CPU core with a dedicated empty GPU. DMControl, Meta-World, and MyoSuite run on an H100 node (2×\times Intel Xeon Gold 6430 CPUs, 2 TB RAM, and 8×\times NVIDIA H100 80GB GPUs); ManiSkill2 on an A100 workstation (AMD EPYC 7V13 CPU, 216 GB RAM, 1×\times A100 80GB).

Appendix I MPPI Planner Warm-Start Strategy Ablation

When the OOD gate triggers a System 1 to System 2 transition after KK timesteps, the planner’s warm-start buffer (_prev_mean) contains a plan that is KK steps stale. We consider two initialization strategies:

  • •

    Cold start: Zero the buffer and discard all stale plans. The MPPI planner relies entirely on the policy prior πθ\pi_{\theta}, which provides Nπ=24N_{\pi}=24 of N=512N=512 candidate trajectories rolled out from the current latent through the world model.

  • •

    KK-shifted warm start: Shift the buffer left by KK positions, salvaging the first H−KH{-}K future plans when K<H−1K<H{-}1. If K≥H−1K\geq H{-}1, no valid plan survives and the strategy degenerates to cold start.

We evaluate both strategies across all 103 tasks from the 4 domains and 8 τ\tau configurations (theoretical: p​50p50, p​75p75, p​90p90, p​95p95, p​99p99; reward-gated: p​25p25, p​50p50, p​75p75), yielding 824 paired comparisons on the clean benchmark and 816 under disturbance. A paired t-test finds no significant difference (p>0.05p>0.05) in return or S2 invocation rate between the two strategies on either benchmark, confirming that the policy prior provides sufficient fresh candidates on S1→\toS2 transitions. We adopt cold start for its simplicity. Tables 26 and 27 report the full results.

Appendix J OOD Distance Metric Ablation

We compare Mahalanobis distance against Tanimoto distance (Rogers and Tanimoto, 1960) as the OOD scoring function. Mahalanobis distance captures the full covariance structure of the in-distribution latents:

gmaha​(zt)=(zt−z¯)⊤​Σreg−1​(zt−z¯),g_{\text{maha}}(z_{t})=(z_{t}-\bar{z})^{\top}\Sigma_{\text{reg}}^{-1}(z_{t}-\bar{z}), (5)

where z¯∈ℝdz\bar{z}\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{z}} is the mean of the ID latents and Σreg=Σ+λ​𝐈\Sigma_{\text{reg}}=\Sigma+\lambda\mathbf{I} is the ℓ2\ell_{2}-regularized covariance (see Section 3), yielding an effective metric that accounts for inter-dimension correlations. Tanimoto distance measures angular and magnitude deviation from the mean without modeling correlations:

gtan​(zt)=1−zt⊤​z¯‖zt‖2+‖z¯‖2−zt⊤​z¯,g_{\text{tan}}(z_{t})=1-\frac{z_{t}^{\top}\bar{z}}{\|z_{t}\|^{2}+\|\bar{z}\|^{2}-z_{t}^{\top}\bar{z}}, (6)

where zt,z¯∈ℝdzz_{t},\bar{z}\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{z}} and the denominator ‖zt‖2+‖z¯‖2−zt⊤​z¯\|z_{t}\|^{2}+\|\bar{z}\|^{2}-z_{t}^{\top}\bar{z} combines Euclidean and inner-product terms into a single similarity ratio. Tanimoto is computationally cheaper (O⁡(dz)O(d_{z}) vs. O⁡(dz2)O(d_{z}^{2}) per step) and requires no covariance inversion during fitting. Both detectors are fitted on the same System 1 rollout trajectories and evaluated under identical τ\tau percentiles.

Tables 28 and 29 report the full results. Under nominal conditions, a paired t-test across all task-config comparisons finds no significant difference in return (t=0.85t{=}0.85, p=0.40p{=}0.40), although Mahalanobis achieves substantially higher success on Meta-World (85% vs. 70% at τp​50\tau_{p50}). In the theoretical mode, Tanimoto yields equal or lower latency at every τ\tau percentile, reflecting fewer S2 invocations; in the reward-gated mode, it is often slower. Under perturbation, Mahalanobis yields significantly higher return (t=2.33t{=}2.33, p=0.02p{=}0.02) by invoking S2 more often. We therefore adopt Mahalanobis for its stronger robustness.

Appendix K Implementation Details

Single configuration. All Fast-TD-MPC components (architecture, training, and OOD detection) use the same hyperparameters across all 103 tasks. No per-task tuning is performed; τ\tau is set automatically for each task-seed from held-out OOD scores using the same rule for all tasks (the median for theoretical mode; the midpoint of the ID and OOD medians for reward-gated mode; see Section 3).

K.1 System 1: Amortized Policy Architecture

Model Architecture.

All components of TD-MPC2 are parameterized by MLPs with LayerNorm and Mish activations. The encoder ℰθ\mathcal{E}_{\theta} and dynamics model 𝒟θ\mathcal{D}_{\theta} additionally use Simplicial Normalization (SimNorm) (Lavoie et al., 2022) on their final layer to normalize the latent representation zz, biasing it towards sparsity without enforcing hard discrete constraints. Mirroring this architecture, the amortized policy πS1\pi_{\text{S1}} is a 4-layer MLP: three intermediate layers of linear →\to LayerNorm →\to Mish, followed by a final SimNorm layer. The backbone takes the frozen latent z∈ℝdzz\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{z}} (dz=512d_{z}=512) as input, maps to a 256-dimensional hidden representation, and a deterministic linear head produces the action. We use history length L=1L=1 and chunk size C=1C=1 (single-step prediction). Following TD-MPC2, actions are squashed with tanh\tanh at the output and dropout (rate 0.1) is applied to the first layer only. We summarize the πS1\pi_{\text{S1}} architecture using PyTorch-like notation:

backbone = SimNormMLPBackbone(
    (0): NormedLinear(512, 256, act=Mish, dropout=0.1)
    (1): NormedLinear(256, 256, act=Mish)
    (2): NormedLinear(256, 256, act=Mish)
    (3): NormedLinear(256, 256, act=SimNorm(dim=8))
)
head = DeterministicHead(
    Linear(256, action_dim)
)

Parameter count. The backbone contains 330,752 parameters; the head contains 256×da+da256\times d_{a}+d_{a} parameters. Total: ∼{\sim}332K for da=6d_{a}=6 (DMControl cheetah) to ∼{\sim}341K for da=39d_{a}=39 (MyoSuite). Compared to TD-MPC2’s 7.9M parameters, this represents a 23×23\times reduction.

K.2 System 1 Training

Expert demonstrations. Expert demonstrations 𝒟exp={(zt,at∗)}\mathcal{D}_{\text{exp}}=\{(z_{t},a^{*}_{t})\} are collected by rolling out the pre-trained TD-MPC2 planner (3 seeds per task, 500 episodes per seed) and recording the latent zt=ℰθ​(st)z_{t}=\mathcal{E}_{\theta}(s_{t}) and the planner’s executed action at∗a^{*}_{t}. Episodes are split 8:1:1 into training, validation, and testing.

Loss. We use L1 loss: ℓ⁡(a^,a∗)=|a^−a∗|\ell(\hat{a},a^{*})=|\hat{a}-a^{*}|, where |a^−a∗||\hat{a}-a^{*}| is the element-wise absolute difference, summed over the action dimension dad_{a}.

Optimizer. AdamW (Loshchilov and Hutter, 2019) with learning rate (lr) 5×10−55\times 10^{-5}, weight decay 10−410^{-4}, betas (0.9,0.999)(0.9,0.999), cosine learning rate schedule with 10% warmup and minimum lr 10−610^{-6}.

Training. Batch size 512, gradient clipping at 1.0, maximum 200 epochs with early stopping (patience 15, minimum delta 10−410^{-4}). All models are trained to full convergence.

K.3 OOD Detector

The OOD detector uses Mahalanobis distance in the frozen encoder’s latent space, operating on dz=512d_{z}=512-dimensional latent features (ztz_{t} with history length L=1L=1). The in-distribution mean z¯\bar{z} and full covariance Σ\Sigma are computed from 400 System 1 rollout episodes per task-seed. We apply ℓ2\ell_{2} shrinkage: Σreg=Σ+λ​𝐈\Sigma_{\text{reg}}=\Sigma+\lambda\mathbf{I} with λ=0.01\lambda=0.01. The scoring function is g⁡(zt)=(zt−z¯)⊤​Σreg−1​(zt−z¯)g(z_{t})=(z_{t}-\bar{z})^{\top}\Sigma_{\text{reg}}^{-1}(z_{t}-\bar{z}). The threshold τ\tau is computed on a separate held-out set of 100 rollout episodes.

We consider two labeling modes for constructing the ID set:

  • •

    Theoretical (all): all visited latents from System 1 rollouts are treated as in-distribution. The threshold τ\tau defaults to the median of g⁡(zt)g(z_{t}) scores on the held-out set.

  • •

    Reward-gated (RG): a state is labeled in-distribution only if its total per-step reward or task completion proxy obtained from the environment meets or exceeds the TD-MPC2 expert’s per-step counterpart at the same timestep. The threshold τ\tau defaults to the midpoint between the median ID and OOD scores.

K.4 System 2

System 2. The MPPI planner (System 2) is used as-is from TD-MPC2, with default hyperparameters: planning horizon H=3H=3, 6 refinement iterations, N=512N=512 samples, Nπ=24N_{\pi}=24 policy-prior trajectories, top-k=64k=64 elite trajectories, min/std 0.050.05/2.02.0, temperature 0.50.5.

Appendix L Extended Related Work

Data-Driven MPC and the TD-MPC Family.

Data-driven model predictive control combines learned world models with online trajectory optimization for planning or data generation. TD-MPC2 (Hansen et al., 2024) combines a task-oriented latent dynamics model with MPPI planning and TD-learning, achieving state-of-the-art performance across 104 continuous control tasks with a single set of hyperparameters, outperforming strong model-free baselines such as SAC (Haarnoja et al., 2018) and model-based methods such as DreamerV3 (Hafner et al., 2025). Its growing ecosystem addresses training efficiency (Evers et al., 2026), humanoid locomotion (Nguyen et al., 2025; Nguyen et al., 2026b), hierarchical planning (Chitnis et al., 2024), policy constraints (Lin et al., 2025a), discrete latent representations (Scannell et al., 2025), and world model reliability (Hansen and Wang, 2026). Concurrent approaches include gradient-based planners that replace sampling-based methods with differentiable optimization (Spieler and Behnke, 2026). Fast-TD-MPC builds directly on the TD-MPC2 framework but, unlike these works, targets inference-time acceleration rather than training improvements or architectural modifications.

Planner Amortization and Speedup.

A natural approach to reducing the cost of online planning is to distill the planner into a lightweight feed-forward policy. Kuzmenko and Shvai (2025) distill a 317M-parameter multi-task TD-MPC2 agent into a smaller quantized model, but MPPI still runs at every step. Wang et al. (2025) learn a policy by imitating an MPC expert via lazy reanalyze, but similarly still execute the planner at deployment, with the policy only seeding the optimization. Nguyen et al. (2026a) replace iterative planning entirely with a goal-conditioned inverse dynamics model, achieving 100-130×\times cost reduction, but provide no fallback when the amortized policy fails on out-of-distribution states. Gao and Xu (2026) accelerate the planner itself by replacing autoregressive latent rollouts with parallel action-prefix prediction, and Huang et al. (2026) amortize iterative planning with a generative flow-matching model; both still execute the full planning loop. Brudermüller et al. (2026) similarly amortize sampling-based MPC via flow matching but always run refinement iterations. Alternative acceleration mechanisms include GPU-parallelized MPC solvers (Bravo-Palacios et al., 2026) and gradient-based MPC in latent space (Spieler and Behnke, 2026), which are orthogonal to our approach. Fast-TD-MPC differs by training a separately amortized policy that can entirely replace the planner on in-distribution states, while retaining the full MPPI planner as a fallback triggered by OOD detection.

Adaptive and Intermittent Replanning.

The idea of conditionally skipping replanning has a long history in classical control theory. Tabuada (2007) introduced event-triggered control, showing that a stabilizing controller need not execute at every timestep but only when a state-dependent condition is violated. Heemels et al. (2012) provided a canonical survey formalizing event-triggered and self-triggered control. Hashimoto et al. (2017) proposed intermittent MPC for nonlinear systems, deliberately skipping replanning when the system is tracking well. This is the closest classical analogue to Fast-TD-MPC’s conditional use of the fast policy.

In the data-driven MPC setting, Cheng et al. (2026) propose AdaReP, a training-free wrapper that adapts replanning tolerance based on model mismatch, achieving over 80% fewer planner queries. However, AdaReP reuses the last cached plan rather than executing a separately learned policy, and its gate is a continuous mismatch threshold rather than a learned OOD detector. Lin et al. (2025b) apply speculative execution — a paradigm originating in LLM inference (Leviathan et al., 2023; Chen et al., 2023), directly to TD-MPC2, generating action queues from the planner’s own latent rollouts and falling back to full replanning on mismatch. This approach is comparable to Fast-TD-MPC, but differs in three key aspects: (i) the fast path uses the planner’s own predictions rather than a separately trained amortized policy, (ii) the gate is a mismatch threshold rather than a learned OOD detector, and (iii) their fast path executes open-loop action queues, whereas Fast-TD-MPC’s System 1 acts closed-loop with per-step OOD gating.

Dual-Process Control and Adaptive Computation.

The dual-process framework of distinguishing a fast, reflexive System 1 from a slow, deliberative System 2 originates in cognitive science (Kahneman, 2011; Daw et al., 2005; Botvinick et al., 2009). A growing body of work adopts this framing for control: Labiosa and Hanna (2026) study learning when to switch between reactive control and deliberative planning, while Li et al. (2026a) learn state-dependent compute schedules for generative control policies. Muppidi et al. (2026) learn planning budgets in real-time RL where the environment does not wait for the agent, directly addressing the think-vs-act trade-off that motivates Fast-TD-MPC. Within the adaptive computation paradigm, Chun et al. (2025) dynamically adjust integration steps for stochastic interpolant policies based on task difficulty, and Salla et al. (2026) learn a prefix-optimal stopping criterion for diffusion policies. Zhao et al. (2026) propose a consistency gate that invokes expensive Best-of-NN selection only when the initial rollout appears internally inconsistent, recovering most of the benefit at a fraction of the cost: a design philosophy shared with Fast-TD-MPC. Concurrent work has proliferated in the VLA domain, including speculation-verification frameworks (Wang et al., 2026), uncertainty-driven “cognitive clutch” mechanisms (Li et al., 2026b), and learned binary gates for cheap/expensive policy switching (Chen, 2026; Liu et al., 2026a). Yan et al. (2026) apply the dual-process framework to motion planning with symbolic solvers as System 2. However, these works operate in VLA, symbolic planning, or diffusion policy domains. Fast-TD-MPC is, to our knowledge, the first to leverage the dual-process framework within MBRL, where the learned world model and MPPI planner provide a principled System 2 that other domains approximate with less grounded alternatives.

Out-of-Distribution Detection in RL.

OOD detection is a mature technique in deep learning (Hendrycks and Gimpel, 2017; Lee et al., 2018), but its application to RL and control settings has received comparatively less attention. Zhang et al. (2024) introduce a distance-based anomaly detection framework for deep RL, directly comparable to our Mahalanobis approach. Kaur et al. (2023) apply conformal OOD detection to time-series data for safety-critical autonomous systems, and Tang and Zhi (2026) use OOD detection to trigger intervention in action-chunking policies — a gating mechanism analogous to Fast-TD-MPC’s, though in the VLA domain. Other works provide formal guarantees for OOD detection in deep RL via transition estimation (Prashant et al., 2025) and benchmark OOD detection methods specifically for RL (Mittag et al., 2026). Fast-TD-MPC repurposes Mahalanobis OOD detection (Lee et al., 2018) as a per-timestep routing mechanism between an amortized policy and a model-based planner — using distributional shift not for anomaly alerting, but as a signal for adaptive compute allocation, a role that, to our knowledge, has not been explored.
